glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
aowliapur-neelkuthi.desc: In the 19th century, British planters forced Bengali farmers to grow indigo, leading to the Indigo Revolt of 1859–60. The ruined neelkuthi at Aowliapur, in Madaripur Sadar upazila, was one of their factory-houses, and parts of its brick walls survive. It is overgrown and unmarked, so ask locals for directions. The quiet ruin tells a story most travellers never hear.
blocks: How to get there
CNG from Madaripur town; ask for Aowliapur neelkuthi.
Good to know
Watch your step around the ruins and in tall grass.

glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
khalia-rajaram-mandir.desc: In Khalia village, Rajoir upazila, stand the remains of the estate of Raja Ram Rai. The temple facade is covered with terracotta panels showing figures, animals and scenes from Hindu epics. The surrounding buildings are partly ruined, and preservation work has been patchy. It is a rewarding stop for anyone who likes Bengal's terracotta art.
blocks: How to get there
Bus or CNG from Madaripur town to Rajoir, then an auto to Khalia.
Good to know
Do not touch the terracotta panels; some are fragile.

madaripur-gachhi-tradition.desc: Date-palm tappers, called gachhis, are central to Madaripur's winter economy. From late autumn they shave the palm trunks, set bamboo pipes and hang clay pots overnight. At dawn they collect the sap and boil it in big pans over earthen stoves until it thickens. The smell of boiling gur drifts across the villages through the cold months.
blocks: Good to know
Avoid drinking raw sap because of Nipah virus risk; taste the boiled gur instead.

glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
charmuguria-eco-park.desc: Charmuguria, near Madaripur town, has long been known for its rhesus monkeys, which live alongside people in the old river-port area. In 2015 the Forest Department made this 4.2-hectare eco-park at Nayachar in Kumarkhali mouza as a sanctuary, hoping to move the monkeys there. Not all of them moved, so you may meet monkeys both in the park and in the bazar lanes. It is a simple, green spot rather than a polished attraction.
blocks: How to get there
Auto or easy-bike from Madaripur town to Charmuguria, then on to Nayachar.
Good to know
Do not feed or tease the monkeys, and keep food and phones out of reach; they snatch. Avoid carrying open snacks.

glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
pranab-math-bajitpur.desc: Bajitpur, west of Madaripur town near the Bhanga–Barishal highway, is where Swami Pranabananda was born. He founded the Bharat Sevashram Sangha, a Hindu monastic and relief organisation, and the Pranab Math here is named after him. Devotees visit the temple and ashram through the year, and it is busiest during his birth anniversary celebrations. It is listed by the district among Rajoir's places of interest, alongside the Khalia Rajaram temple not far away.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Madaripur toward Rajoir and get off at Bajitpur on the Bhanga–Barishal highway; the math is close to the road.
Good to know
Take off your shoes at the temple. You can combine it with the Khalia Rajaram temple in Rajoir the same day.

glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
madaripur-museum.desc: Madaripur Museum was opened by the district administration in March 2023 in the old treasury building beside Shakuni Lake. The building itself is part of the story: in March 1971 the sub-divisional officer handed weapons from this treasury to local freedom fighters. The galleries cover the district's history, from the anti-British movements and the Language Movement to the Liberation War. It is a small museum and fits easily into an evening walk around the lake.
blocks: How to get there
Walk or take a rickshaw to Shakuni Lake in Madaripur town; the museum is on the lake's north side.
Good to know
Check opening days locally before going. Pair it with a walk around Shakuni Lake.

madaripur-khirpuri.desc: Khirpuri is made from milk boiled down for hours into thick khir and shaped into soft, rich pieces. Madaripur's sweet makers are famous for it, and boxes are carried to Dhaka and even abroad. It tastes deeply milky with a hint of caramel. Sweet shops in Madaripur town also sell good rasgolla and chhanar jilapi.

glance: Village makers and winter haats around Madaripur
madaripur-khejur-gur.desc: Madaripur is one of the districts best known for khejur gur. In winter, sap from date palms is boiled into runny jhola gur or set into firm patali cakes. Its smoky sweetness flavours payesh, pitha and winter tea across the region. Buy from makers or trusted shops to avoid sugar-adulterated gur.

glance: 105 km to Madaripur by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
shakuni-lake.desc: Shakuni Lake is the green heart of Madaripur town, a long rectangular lake surrounded by walkways and shade trees. In the late afternoon families, students and tea sellers gather along its banks. Government buildings and the town's memorials line parts of the shore. It is the easiest place to get a feel for daily life in the town.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from anywhere in Madaripur town.

madaripur-ilish-bhaja.desc: The south-bank ghats at Shibchar developed the same fried-hilsa tradition as Mawa across the river. Pick a fish, and it is cut into steaks and fried in mustard oil until crisp. It comes with rice, fried roe and green chillies. It is best in the monsoon hilsa season.

shibchar-padma-riverside.desc: Shibchar upazila lies on the south bank of the Padma, close to the south end of the Padma Bridge. Before the bridge, the Kathalbari and Banglabazar ferry ghats here were among the busiest in the country. Today the riverbank is calmer, with views of the bridge and boats heading out to fish for hilsa. The ghat eateries still fry fresh fish for visitors.
blocks: How to get there
Bus via the Padma Bridge expressway to Shibchar, then an auto to the riverside.
Good to know
River currents are strong; only take boats with life jackets.
